A1.justification: Despite the changed title and extensive reorganization, both PDFs describe VIM and Inter-MT2. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion reasoning, editing, generation, dataset-quality, and ablation results, including a 30-participant user study.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental and user-study results and reports additional baseline comparisons, tokenizer sensitivity results, and qualitative demonstrations.

M1.justification: v4 adds an incremental inference procedure for group interactions: generate two-person motion, generate another person's reaction conditioned on existing motion, and merge the outputs (Section 5.5 and Appendix D). The underlying RQ-VAE tokenizer, LLaMA backbone, and three-stage training pipeline remain.

E1.justification: The training datasets and principal tasks remain unchanged. v4 adds a three-person interaction demonstration and a longer-conversation test case (Figure 8 and Figure P.11), extending the tested scenarios without introducing a new training dataset.

E2.justification: v4 adds MoMask* to text-to-motion and reaction-generation comparisons, and ComMDM to text-to-motion comparisons (Table 4 and Appendix F). TM2T* and InterGEN were already evaluated in v1 Tables 8–9; their appearance in the main comparison is largely relocation.

E3.justification: v4 drops ROUGE-L from motion-reasoning evaluation and replaces the detailed synthesized-subset quality comparison with an Inter-MT2 retrieval/diversity summary. Its new reconstruction study varies codebook size from 128 to 1024 and depth from 2 to 5. The reported dataset split and user-study design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 substantially extends the analyses with a systematic codebook-size/depth sweep, a three-person generation case study, and an explicit failure during a longer conversation (Figure C.1, Appendix D, and Figure P.11). The original pretraining and VQ-versus-RQ ablations are retained as Tables B.1 and C.2.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same repeated-measures MANOVA, post-hoc comparisons, significance thresholds, and 95% confidence intervals for the user study. Neither adds training-run counts, seed information, or uncertainty estimates for the automated benchmark results.

E6.justification: Most shared scores remain unchanged, including VIM's reasoning coherence of 5.252 and editing FID of 0.064. v4 adds baseline scores, expanded reaction metrics, sensitivity results, and qualitative findings, while removing reasoning ROUGE-L entries. Its Inter-MT2 quality scores of 0.701 retrieval and 0.931 diversity replace v1's synthesized-subset scores of 0.668 and 0.824; these do not establish a same-setting improvement. Some new results conflict internally, such as ComMDM retrieval of 0.251 in Table 4 versus 0.201 in Table F.4.

T1.justification: The motion representation, residual-quantization mathematics, and basic training formulation are retained. Added token-format explanations document implementation rather than introducing substantive mathematical definitions, derivations, propositions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The model, dataset, and evaluation-protocol contributions remain. v4's abstract adds an explicit claim to being the first unified model addressing all the listed tasks and adds competitive performance against task-specific methods to its principal claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of codebook saturation and efficiency, argues for extending interactions to groups through iterative conditioning, and identifies a concrete longer-conversation failure. The existing limitations concerning unseen actions, long token sequences, and personalization remain, relocated to Appendix G.

D1.justification: v4 newly explains duplicated encoder inputs and omission of second-person tokens for single-person training, and baseline token interleaving (Appendices A, H, and I). It also discloses 2,002 reasoning and 1,445 editing evaluation samples and promises release of data, code, and models. These disclosures do not establish changed experiments or actual resource availability.

R1.justification: v4 adds the in2in citation and removes references to FineMoGEN, the original VQ-VAE paper, and ROUGE. It more explicitly positions VIM as a unified alternative to unidirectional methods, while retaining the principal related-work categories and comparisons.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and substantial portions of the introduction, methods, and experimental narrative are rewritten. The appendix is extensively reorganized; tokenizer ablations and limitations move out of the main text, while multi-person generation receives a new main-text subsection.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column layout, with substantially redrawn overview and qualitative figures. v4 adds dataset charts, a tokenizer diagram, sensitivity plots, and group-generation and failure illustrations. Existing pipeline figures, ablation tables, and supplementary comparisons are relocated or restructured.

improvement.justification: The added baseline comparisons, tokenizer sensitivity study, explicit failure example, and implementation disclosures modestly strengthen validation and transparency beyond v1. The gains are limited by inconsistent new reporting: Appendix F.2 claims MoMask retrieval of 0.844, whereas Table F.4 reports 0.612, and some main/appendix scores disagree. Broader group-generation claims also rest on a qualitative example. The revision improves the paper, but does not establish a substantial overall advance in its evidential quality.
